title: Trailer Heist Foiled: Thieves Get 40,000 Pounds of Sand Instead of Tech
summary:
In a twist that sounds like a comedy sketch, thieves in California stole two trailers bearing the logos of PlusAI and Nvidia—only to discover they were filled with 40,000 pounds of sand. The incident happened on Thursday morning near Newark, California.

A top executive at PlusAI, a self-driving truck developer, received a congratulatory text from an acquaintance who had spotted two of the company's trailers near their office. But those trailers were supposed to be docked outside PlusAI's warehouse, half a mile away. Soon, police were on the scene to recover the trailers.

PlusAI employees explained why the thieves might have abandoned the trailers after breaking them open: each contained about 20,000 pounds of sand. "PlusAI uses simulated loads in its trailers to assist with research and development testing," said Lauren Kwan, a company spokesperson. The trailers were recovered with "40,000 pounds of sand intact." The tech-enabled truck cabs—where the driver sits—were parked inside the warehouse and weren't taken. The trailers had been secured with hand locks, which were broken.

The case is under investigation, and no arrests have been made, according to Amy Gee, a spokesperson for the Fremont Police Department. Nvidia declined to comment.

This incident comes amid a rise in theft targeting high-value computer equipment, especially chips and electronics for data centers. In August, WIRED reported two California incidents where thieves struck vehicles of security escorts following high-value tech loads. Millions of dollars of data center equipment remain unrecovered. Thieves have also targeted Tesla batteries and bitcoin mining machines. Common cargo theft targets include metals and enterprise-grade computer equipment, according to Verisk CargoNet.

Fortunately, this story has a happier ending: by Thursday afternoon, the sand trailers were back with PlusAI.
why_it_matters: Supply chains carrying AI hardware have become a strategic target, so how companies and police protect cargo affects the price and availability of the technology that increasingly runs schools, hospitals and whole economies.

background_read: Cargo theft — stealing goods while they are being moved by truck, train or ship — is a long-running problem in the United States, especially along busy freight corridors such as California's Interstate 5. Organised crews often follow loaded trucks, cut locks at stops, and resell the goods through informal networks.

Verisk CargoNet (a company that collects and analyses reports of stolen cargo for insurers and shipping firms) tracks which goods thieves prefer. It says metals and high-end computer equipment are among the most common targets because they are valuable, easy to resell and hard to trace.

Nvidia (the company that designs the powerful chips used to train artificial intelligence) sits at the centre of the boom in data centers — giant buildings full of servers. Because those chips are scarce and expensive, they have become a prime target for organised theft.

PlusAI is a California company developing self-driving truck technology, and its trailers carried the logos of both companies. The incident happened near Newark, California, in the San Francisco Bay Area, and is being investigated by the Fremont Police Department (the local police force in the neighbouring city).

perspectives.description: The trailers were recovered with their contents intact the same day, nobody was hurt, and the case is now in police hands. PlusAI also gained worldwide publicity for its self-driving truck testing programme.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — logistics insurers and security experts
perspectives.description: They point out that this 'funny' story sits inside a serious trend: organised crews are targeting electronics and data-center gear, and millions of dollars of stolen equipment is never recovered. Those losses are eventually paid for by companies and, often, by customers.

Cargo theft is as old as trade, but what has changed is the value density of what moves: one pallet of AI chips can be worth more than a whole truckload of televisions. This case shows that a logo alone signals value to thieves, even when the trailer is empty of anything they want.

The next steps are likely better tracking and protection: GPS trackers, sealed loads, escorted convoys and faster reporting when trailers go missing. As long as AI hardware stays scarce and expensive, thieves will keep following the freight.
